(A) One feature of the workshop is that several workers are doing different jobs at once. In the foreground one man inks the type form with two ink balls while another raises the hinged frame of the big wooden screw press, and in the background a worker sits at a type case setting type. This shows that printed works were made through a division of labor, with each step done by a different person so the shop could turn out many copies of the same sheet.

(B) One development that explains the spread of these workshops is Johannes Gutenberg's development of movable-type printing in Mainz around 1450. His method of using reusable metal type with a press made books much faster and cheaper to produce than hand-copied manuscripts, so printers trained in the technique moved to other cities. By 1500 there were presses in many cities, such as Venice and Paris, because merchants saw printing as a profitable business, and Renaissance humanists and universities wanted copies of classical texts.

(C) One effect of printing on religious life was the fast spread of Martin Luther's ideas during the Protestant Reformation. After Luther wrote the Ninety-Five Theses in 1517, his pamphlets and his German translation of the Bible were printed in large numbers and spread across the German states far faster than the Church could suppress them. This helped Protestantism gain followers, and the Catholic Church answered by creating the Index of Prohibited Books to control what Catholics could read.
